items.title: Jon Weber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 2, 2012
items.q: And Duke Ellington for example, thought horizontally.

ctx.x: You know there’s nothing like that feeling, pre-Finale or Sibelius, of writing a piece, and you know you check it at the piano, but you’re never really sure it’s going to work until all those human beings get there and they read it.

You’re right, and there are people who write vertically and there are people who write horizontally. I mean Mancini for example writes vertically, meaning you could take any cross section of any conductor’s score and it’s going to be a fabulous chord. He thinks that way, he thinks vertically. And Duke Ellington for example, thought horizontally. Everybody’s line had to be something really hip. And it somehow works horizontally. And I don’t know if anybody ever analyzed it that way. Maybe this is the advantage of…

I think that’s a great point. Because I remember listening to him some recently and I was trying to figure out what is it that make him sound like he does. And that’s a very good sort of observation. And what you just said too. What did you just say?
